<reason>The pivotal exchange was CON's dilemma about the app-lock: either the lock is cheap/costless (so a cap is easy to enforce) or it's expensive infrastructure funded by price-linked fees (so capping fees degrades it). PRO's A1/A2 answers tried to have both — claiming the lock is "a switch platforms already own" while simultaneously arguing fees don't track cost — but never actually resolved why stripping fee revenue wouldn't weaken enforcement capacity, which CON hammered again in Rebuttal 2 and Closing. CON's framing that the surplus doesn't vanish but relocates (to bots at primary sale, off-app brokers, or DM handoffs) was never fully neutralized; PRO's response that "fans will prefer the guaranteed in-app ticket" is plausible but asserted rather than demonstrated against CON's specific migration mechanisms (shared logins, meet-outside handoffs). PRO's rebuttal that a percentage fee is "the tell" of extraction rather than insurance is a decent point but doesn't answer why competitive platforms haven't already undercut each other on fees if the lock truly is cheap, a question CON raised effectively in closing. Both sides argued well and PRO's rhetoric was slightly sharper and more memorable ("Want ten times? Find another business"), but CON's core enforcement/funding contradiction went more thoroughly unanswered by the end, giving CON the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.1/B4.4 dilemma — that PRO's mandate requires the app-lock to be simultaneously strong enough to enforce a cap and irrelevant enough to survive defunding — which PRO's A4 answers asserted around but never structurally resolved.</best_rebuttal>
